title: A New Earth
sources: https://www.ikhtyar.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/eckhart-tolle-a-new-earth.pdf (full text hosted by a third party, read directly: ch. 2, 3, 5, 6, 7)

facts.claim: Tolle's own first glimpse: as a first-year student at the University of London, aged 25 ('a mature first-year student'), he rode the tube twice a week to the library. A woman in her early thirties sat opposite him, the seats on both sides of her empty, talking to herself 'incessantly in a loud and angry voice' in an imaginary argument ('...so I said to her you are a liar how dare you accuse me of...').

She got off at Tottenham Court Road and walked toward Bedford Square still arguing. He followed her at about twenty steps; she was heading for Senate House, the university library building, where he was going too, and she disappeared into an elevator.

In the men's room before entering the library, washing his hands, he thought 'I hope I don't end up like her', then realised he had mumbled it aloud and the man next to him glanced over. He thought: 'Oh my God, I'm already like her.' His mind was as incessantly active as hers; her underlying emotion seemed anger, his anxiety; she thought out loud, he thought in his head.

Then, for a moment, he stood back from his own mind and saw it from a deeper perspective, a brief shift from thinking to awareness. Looking at his face in the mirror he laughed out loud: 'Life isn't as serious as my mind makes it out to be.' Tolle calls it only a glimpse, quickly forgotten; he spent the next three years in anxiety and depression, and awareness returned later, after he got close to suicide.

What the 'I' identifies with, per Tolle: roles (mother, father, husband, wife), accumulated knowledge or opinions, likes and dislikes, and things that happened to 'me' in the past, memories that define 'me and my story'. These are 'no more than thoughts held together precariously'. Most people are completely identified with the stream of compulsive thinking; told there is a voice in their head they say 'What voice?', which is the voice.

Practice: 'See if you can catch, that is to say, notice, the voice in the head, perhaps in the very moment it complains about something.' Whenever you notice the voice, you realise you are not the voice but the one who is aware of it. In the background there is awareness, in the foreground the voice, the thinker. Each time it is recognised, the pattern is weakened.
Tolle's soup example: telling the waiter your soup is cold is not ego if you stick to the facts; 'How dare you serve me cold soup...' is complaining in the service of the ego, not of change.

Pain-body: any negative emotion not fully faced and let go leaves a remnant of pain; remnants join into an energy field living in the cells of the body, 'an accumulation of old emotional pain', which Tolle calls the pain-body. Children often cannot face strong emotions, and the defence usually remains in adulthood.

The pain-body has a dormant and an active stage; dormant can last a few weeks (most common), days, months, rarely years. It wakes when hungry or when triggered, and 'can use the most insignificant event as a trigger, something somebody says or does, or even a thought'. Alone, it feeds on your thoughts, which turn negative; with others, 'preferably your partner or a close family member', it provokes them to feed on the drama.
Tolle describes it as 'a semiautonomous energy form', with a primitive intelligence 'not unlike a cunning animal' aimed at survival, 'an addiction to unhappiness'.

Relationships: 'You don't just marry your wife or husband, you also marry her or his pain-body.' Example given: not long after moving in together, a partner's voice turns harsh or she accuses or shouts, 'most likely over a relatively trivial matter', or goes withdrawn; asked what is wrong she says 'Nothing', while the hostile energy says 'Everything is wrong'; Tolle says it is the pain-body speaking through her, not the real face.

People with dense pain-bodies blow insignificant matters up 'out of all proportion' and cannot tell the difference between an event and their reaction to the event. Tolle's examples include road rage over someone driving too slowly.

Ch. 6 'Breaking Free': freedom begins with realising you have a pain-body and with being present enough to notice it 'as a heavy influx of negative emotion when it becomes active. When it is recognized, it can no longer pretend to be you'. It does not usually dissolve immediately, but once the link to your thinking is cut it begins to lose energy.

Present moment (ch. 7): 'there is only ever this moment. Life is always now.' Past and future moments exist only when you remember or anticipate them, and you do that by thinking in 'the only moment there is: this one'. Tolle calls the apparent plurality of moments a confusion of the present moment with what happens in it.

Tolle names three ways the ego treats the present moment: as a means to an end (never fully here because always busy getting elsewhere), as an obstacle (impatience, frustration, stress; life becomes a problem to solve before you can be happy), or as an enemy (hating what you are doing, complaining, inner dialogue of shoulds and blaming).

Tolle's question: 'What is my relationship with the present moment?' with three checks: 'Am I treating the Now as no more than a means to an end? Do I see it as an obstacle? Am I making it into an enemy?' Noticing the dysfunction is itself presence; 'with the seeing comes the power of choice.' Ask it often 'until you don't need it anymore'.

Tolle's time example: he met old friends after almost thirty years; the mother walked with a cane, the daughter, once full of energy, looked worn out after bringing up three children. 'Time had done this to them.' Yet 'everything seems to be subject to time, yet it all happens in the Now', and you never experience time itself, only the present moment. Clock time is useful for practical purposes; he objects to 'psychological time', preoccupation with past and future.

rejected.claim: Old 1663: a question 'Who are you?' with the answers name, job, roles, history, thoughts; 'all real but not you'.
rejected.reason: Book lists what the 'I' identifies with (f5) but does not say they are 'all real'. Rewritten around Tolle's tube story.

rejected.claim: Old 1663: 'the awareness is free, a space where thoughts come and go'; 'start of liberation'.
rejected.reason: Tolle's wording is f6. The 'space' and 'start of liberation' framing not used.

rejected.reason: Examples invented. Book's examples are f11, f12.
